notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Life science is the branch of science dealing with living organisms and life processes.
  • Biology is the major science concerned with living organisms.
  • The word biology is derived from Greek words bios meaning life and logos meaning study.
  • Living organisms show organisation, metabolism, growth, reproduction, response to stimuli and regulation.
  • The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
  • All organisms are composed of one or more cells.
  • Life depends on interactions among genes, cells, organisms and the environment.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Biology → Study of Life

Cell → Basic Unit of Life

2. Major Branches of Biology

Important branches include:

  • Botany → Study of plants.
  • Zoology → Study of animals.
  • Microbiology → Study of microorganisms.
  • Cytology → Study of cells.
  • Histology → Study of tissues.
  • Anatomy → Study of structure.
  • Physiology → Study of functions.
  • Genetics → Study of heredity and variation.
  • Ecology → Study of organisms and environment.
  • Evolutionary biology → Study of biological evolution.
3. Botany
  • Botany deals with plants.
  • It includes plant structure, physiology, reproduction, classification and ecology.
  • Theophrastus is traditionally called the Father of Botany.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Theophrastus → Father of Botany

4. Zoology
  • Zoology deals with animals.
  • It includes animal anatomy, physiology, classification, behaviour and evolution.
  • Aristotle is traditionally called the Father of Zoology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aristotle → Father of Zoology

5. Characteristics of Living Organisms

Living organisms generally show:

  • Cellular organisation.
  • Metabolism.
  • Growth.
  • Reproduction.
  • Respiration.
  • Nutrition.
  • Excretion.
  • Response to stimuli.
  • Homeostasis.
  • Adaptation.
  • Heredity.
  • Evolution.
6. Cellular Organisation
  • All known living organisms are made of cells.
  • Unicellular organisms consist of a single cell.
  • Multicellular organisms contain many specialised cells.
  • Cells perform essential biochemical processes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

All Living Organisms → Cellular Organisation

7. Unicellular Organisms

Examples include:

  • Amoeba.
  • Paramecium.
  • Many bacteria.
  • Many yeasts.
  • Chlamydomonas.
  • A single cell performs all essential life functions.
8. Multicellular Organisms
  • Multicellular organisms contain many cells.
  • Cells become specialised for different functions.
  • Similar cells form tissues.
  • Tissues form organs.
  • Organs form organ systems.
📌 Organisation Chain

Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ System → Organism

9. Metabolism
  • Metabolism is the sum total of chemical reactions occurring in a living organism.
  • Metabolism includes anabolism and catabolism.
  • Enzymes regulate metabolic reactions.
  • Metabolism requires controlled energy transfer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Metabolism = Anabolism + Catabolism

10. Anabolism
  • Anabolism includes constructive metabolic reactions.
  • Simple molecules are combined to form complex molecules.
  • Energy is generally required.
  • Protein synthesis is anabolic.
  • Photosynthesis is broadly anabolic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anabolism → Building Up

11. Catabolism
  • Catabolism includes breakdown reactions.
  • Complex molecules are broken into simpler molecules.
  • Energy is generally released.
  • Cellular respiration is catabolic.
  • Digestion contains catabolic processes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Catabolism → Breaking Down

12. Growth
  • Growth is an irreversible increase in size, mass or cell number.
  • Multicellular organisms grow mainly through cell division and cell enlargement.
  • Plants often continue growing throughout life at meristems.
  • Animal growth is generally more determinate.
13. Reproduction
  • Reproduction produces new individuals.
  • It ensures continuity of a species.
  • Reproduction can be asexual or sexual.
  • Reproduction is not essential for survival of an individual organism but is essential for long-term continuation of a species.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Reproduction is not a defining requirement for every individual living organism because sterile individuals can still be alive.

14. Response to Stimuli
  • Living organisms respond to changes in their surroundings.
  • A stimulus is a detectable environmental or internal change.
  • Plants respond to light, gravity and touch.
  • Animals respond through nervous and hormonal mechanisms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stimulus → Response

15. Homeostasis
  • Homeostasis is maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment.
  • Body temperature, blood glucose and water balance are regulated homeostatically.
  • Homeostasis depends on feedback mechanisms.
  • Claude Bernard and Walter Cannon are important historical figures in the development of homeostasis concepts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Homeostasis → Stable Internal Environment

16. Adaptation
  • Adaptation is an inherited characteristic that improves survival or reproductive success in a particular environment.
  • Adaptations arise over generations through evolution.
  • Individual short-term adjustment is better described as acclimatisation rather than evolutionary adaptation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Adaptation → Population-level inherited evolutionary feature.

Acclimatisation → Individual physiological adjustment.

17. Nutrition
  • Nutrition is obtaining and using substances needed for energy, growth and repair.
  • Organisms may be autotrophic or heterotrophic.
  • Plants generally show autotrophic nutrition through photosynthesis.
  • Animals show heterotrophic nutrition.
18. Autotrophic Nutrition
  • Autotrophs manufacture organic food from inorganic substances.
  • Green plants use light energy.
  • Carbon dioxide and water are raw materials of photosynthesis.
  • Photosynthetic organisms form the base of many food chains.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Autotroph → Makes Own Organic Food

19. Heterotrophic Nutrition
  • Heterotrophs depend on other organisms or organic matter for food.
  • Animals are heterotrophs.
  • Fungi are heterotrophs.
  • Many bacteria are heterotrophs.
20. Modes of Heterotrophic Nutrition

Important modes include:

  • Holozoic.
  • Saprotrophic.
  • Parasitic.
  • Symbiotic.
21. Holozoic Nutrition
  • Holozoic organisms ingest solid or liquid food.
  • Food is digested internally.
  • Humans and many animals show holozoic nutrition.
  • Amoeba also shows holozoic nutrition.
22. Saprotrophic Nutrition
  • Saprotrophs obtain nutrients from dead and decaying organic matter.
  • They secrete digestive enzymes outside the body.
  • Soluble nutrients are then absorbed.
  • Many fungi show saprotrophic nutrition.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fungi → Common Saprotrophs

23. Parasitic Nutrition
  • Parasites obtain nutrients from a living host.
  • The host is harmed to some degree.
  • Tapeworm is an animal parasite.
  • Cuscuta is a parasitic plant.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cuscuta → Parasitic Plant

24. Symbiosis
  • Symbiosis is a close association between different species.
  • In mutualism, both partners benefit.
  • Lichen is an association between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner.
  • Mycorrhiza is an association between fungi and plant roots.
25. Respiration
  • Respiration releases usable energy from food molecules.
  • Cellular respiration occurs within cells.
  • Aerobic respiration uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
  • Anaerobic pathways operate without oxygen.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Respiration ≠ Breathing.

Breathing is gas movement.

Cellular respiration is biochemical energy release.

26. Aerobic Respiration
  • Aerobic respiration uses oxygen.
  • Glucose is oxidised mainly to carbon dioxide and water.
  • Large amounts of ATP are produced.
  • In eukaryotes, most aerobic ATP production occurs in mitochondria.
📌 Simplified Equation

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + Energy

27. Anaerobic Respiration / Fermentation
  • Anaerobic energy pathways occur without oxygen.
  • Yeast can convert glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide.
  • Animal muscle under low-oxygen conditions can produce lactate.
  • Anaerobic pathways yield much less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
28. Excretion
  • Excretion removes metabolic waste products.
  • Carbon dioxide is an excretory product.
  • Nitrogenous wastes include ammonia, urea and uric acid.
  • Excretion helps maintain internal chemical balance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Excretion ≠ Egestion.

Excretion → Metabolic waste.

Egestion → Undigested food removal.

29. Cell — Basic Definition
  • Cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
  • Cells are enclosed by a plasma membrane.
  • Cells contain genetic material.
  • Cells carry out metabolism.
  • Cells arise from pre-existing cells.
30. Discovery of the Cell
  • Robert Hooke observed thin slices of cork in 1665.
  • He saw box-like compartments.
  • He called them cells.
  • Hooke observed dead cell walls, not living protoplasm.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Robert Hooke → Cell → 1665

31. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
  • Antonie van Leeuwenhoek observed living microscopic organisms.
  • He improved simple microscopes.
  • He observed bacteria, protozoa and sperm cells.
  • He is often called the Father of Microbiology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Leeuwenhoek → Living Microorganisms

32. Cell Theory

Classical cell theory states:

  • All living organisms are made of cells.
  • Cell is the basic unit of structure and function.
  • New cells arise from pre-existing cells.
33. Schleiden
  • Matthias Schleiden concluded that plants are composed of cells.
  • His work was published in 1838.
  • He contributed to development of cell theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Schleiden → Plants Made of Cells

34. Schwann
  • Theodor Schwann concluded that animals are made of cells.
  • He extended cell theory to animals in 1839.
  • Schleiden and Schwann are jointly associated with cell theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Schwann → Animals Made of Cells

35. Rudolf Virchow
  • Rudolf Virchow popularised the principle that every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.
  • The Latin phrase is Omnis cellula e cellula.
  • This completed an important part of classical cell theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Virchow → Cells from Pre-existing Cells

36. Prokaryotic Cell
  • Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
  • Their DNA lies in a nucleoid region.
  • They lack membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and Golgi apparatus.
  • Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes.
  • Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Prokaryote → No True Membrane-Bound Nucleus

37. Eukaryotic Cell
  • Eukaryotic cells possess a membrane-bound nucleus.
  • They contain membrane-bound organelles.
  • Plants, animals, fungi and protists are eukaryotes.
  • Their chromosomes are located inside the nucleus.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Eukaryote → True Nucleus + Membrane-Bound Organelles

38. Prokaryote vs Eukaryote
  • Prokaryote → Nucleoid.
  • Eukaryote → Nucleus.
  • Prokaryote → No membrane-bound organelles.
  • Eukaryote → Membrane-bound organelles present.
  • Prokaryotic ribosomes → 70S.
  • Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes → 80S.
📌 Must-Memorise

Prokaryote → 70S

Eukaryote Cytoplasm → 80S

39. Plasma Membrane
  • Plasma membrane surrounds the cell.
  • It separates cell contents from the environment.
  • It is selectively permeable.
  • It consists mainly of phospholipids and proteins.
  • It controls movement of substances into and out of the cell.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Plasma Membrane → Selectively Permeable

40. Fluid Mosaic Model
  • Fluid mosaic model describes the structure of biological membranes.
  • It was proposed by S. J. Singer and G. L. Nicolson in 1972.
  • Phospholipids form a fluid bilayer.
  • Proteins are embedded within or attached to the bilayer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Singer + Nicolson → Fluid Mosaic Model → 1972

41. Cell Wall
  • Plant cells possess a cell wall outside the plasma membrane.
  • Plant cell walls contain cellulose.
  • Fungal cell walls contain mainly chitin.
  • Bacterial cell walls commonly contain peptidoglycan.
  • Animal cells do not possess cell walls.
📌 Must-Memorise

Plant → Cellulose

Fungus → Chitin

Bacterium → Peptidoglycan

42. Cytoplasm
  • Cytoplasm is the material between plasma membrane and nucleus in eukaryotic cells.
  • It contains cytosol and organelles.
  • Many metabolic reactions occur in cytoplasm.
  • Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol.
43. Nucleus
  • Nucleus contains most of the genetic material in eukaryotic cells.
  • It is surrounded by a double nuclear envelope.
  • Nuclear pores regulate transport.
  • Chromatin is present inside.
  • The nucleolus is involved in ribosome production.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nucleus → Genetic Control Centre

44. Nucleolus
  • Nucleolus is a dense region inside the nucleus.
  • It synthesises ribosomal RNA.
  • Ribosomal subunits begin assembly there.
  • It is not surrounded by its own membrane.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nucleolus → Ribosome Formation

45. Chromatin
  • Chromatin is DNA associated with proteins.
  • It condenses to form visible chromosomes during cell division.
  • Histone proteins are major chromosome-associated proteins in eukaryotes.
46. Chromosome
  • Chromosomes are structures carrying genetic information.
  • They are composed mainly of DNA and proteins.
  • Genes are located on chromosomes.
  • Chromosome number is species-specific.
47. Human Chromosome Number
  • Human somatic cells normally contain 46 chromosomes.
  • They occur as 23 pairs.
  • 22 pairs are autosomes.
  • One pair consists of sex chromosomes.
  • Human gametes contain 23 chromosomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Human Somatic Cell → 46

Human Gamete → 23

48. Mitochondria
  • Mitochondria are sites of most aerobic ATP production in eukaryotic cells.
  • They possess a double membrane.
  • Inner membrane forms cristae.
  • They contain their own DNA.
  • They contain 70S-like ribosomes.
  • Mitochondria are often called the powerhouses of the cell.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mitochondria → ATP / Powerhouse

49. Chloroplast
  • Chloroplasts are present in plants and many algae.
  • They carry out photosynthesis.
  • Chlorophyll is located in thylakoid membranes.
  • Chloroplasts have their own DNA.
  • They contain 70S-like ribosomes.
  • They are double-membrane organelles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chloroplast → Photosynthesis

50. Endosymbiotic Theory
  • Endosymbiotic theory explains the evolutionary origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts.
  • It proposes that ancestral eukaryotic cells incorporated free-living bacteria.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts retain their own DNA and bacterial-type ribosomes.
  • Lynn Margulis strongly developed and popularised this theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Endosymbiosis → Mitochondria + Chloroplast Origin

51. Ribosome
  • Ribosomes are sites of protein synthesis.
  • They are made of ribosomal RNA and proteins.
  • Ribosomes are not membrane-bound.
  • Free ribosomes make many cytosolic proteins.
  • Ribosomes attached to rough ER make many secreted and membrane proteins.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ribosome → Protein Synthesis

52. Endoplasmic Reticulum

Two main forms are:

  • Rough endoplasmic reticulum.
  • Smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
  • ER is a membrane network within eukaryotic cells.
53. Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum
  • Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface.
  • It participates in synthesis of proteins destined for secretion or membranes.
  • It also assists protein folding and modification.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rough ER → Protein Synthesis

54. Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum
  • Smooth ER lacks surface ribosomes.
  • It participates in lipid synthesis.
  • It contributes to detoxification.
  • It stores calcium in specialised muscle cells.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Smooth ER → Lipids + Detoxification

55. Golgi Apparatus
  • Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids.
  • It forms transport vesicles.
  • It is important in secretion.
  • Camillo Golgi discovered the organelle.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Golgi → Packaging and Secretion

56. Lysosome
  • Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes.
  • They break down macromolecules and worn-out cellular components.
  • They function in intracellular digestion.
  • Christian de Duve discovered lysosomes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lysosome → Intracellular Digestion

57. Peroxisome
  • Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes.
  • They break down fatty acids.
  • Catalase in peroxisomes decomposes hydrogen peroxide.
  • They help detoxify harmful oxidative products.
📌 Reaction

2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

58. Vacuole
  • Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs.
  • Plant cells often contain a large central vacuole.
  • It stores water, ions, pigments and wastes.
  • It helps maintain turgor pressure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Plant Central Vacuole → Turgor

59. Centrosome
  • Centrosome is an important microtubule-organising centre in animal cells.
  • It contains a pair of centrioles in many animal cells.
  • It helps organise the spindle during cell division.
  • Higher plant cells generally lack typical centrioles.
60. Cytoskeleton

The cytoskeleton includes:

  • Microtubules.
  • Microfilaments.
  • Intermediate filaments.
  • It maintains cell shape.
  • It assists movement and intracellular transport.
  • It participates in cell division.
61. Cilia
  • Cilia are short hair-like projections from cells.
  • They help move cells or move materials across cell surfaces.
  • Cilia in the respiratory tract help move mucus.
  • Paramecium moves using cilia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Paramecium → Cilia

62. Flagellum
  • Flagella are longer whip-like structures.
  • They help in cell movement.
  • Human sperm moves using a flagellum.
  • Euglena also possesses a flagellum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sperm → Flagellum

63. Plant Cell vs Animal Cell

Plant cell generally has:

  • Cell wall.
  • Chloroplasts in photosynthetic tissues.
  • Large central vacuole.

Animal cell generally has:

  • No cell wall.
  • No chloroplast.
  • Smaller vacuoles.
  • Typical centrosome with centrioles.
64. Biomolecules

Major biological molecules include:

  • Carbohydrates.
  • Proteins.
  • Lipids.
  • Nucleic acids.
  • Vitamins.
  • Water and minerals are also essential biological components.
65. Carbohydrates
  • Carbohydrates contain mainly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
  • They are important energy sources.
  • Glucose is a major cellular fuel.
  • Starch is a storage carbohydrate in plants.
  • Glycogen is a storage carbohydrate in animals.
  • Cellulose forms plant cell walls.
📌 Must-Memorise

Plant Storage → Starch

Animal Storage → Glycogen

Plant Cell Wall → Cellulose

66. Monosaccharides

Important monosaccharides include:

  • Glucose.
  • Fructose.
  • Galactose.
  • Ribose.
  • Deoxyribose.
  • Monosaccharides are simple sugars.
67. Disaccharides

Important examples:

  • Sucrose → Glucose + Fructose.
  • Lactose → Glucose + Galactose.
  • Maltose → Glucose + Glucose.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sucrose → Cane/Table Sugar

Lactose → Milk Sugar

Maltose → Malt Sugar

68. Polysaccharides

Important polysaccharides include:

  • Starch.
  • Glycogen.
  • Cellulose.
  • Chitin.
  • They are long polymers of sugar units.
69. Protein
  • Proteins are polymers of amino acids.
  • Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds.
  • Proteins perform structural, enzymatic, transport and regulatory functions.
  • Most enzymes are proteins.
  • Haemoglobin is a protein.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Protein → Amino Acids

70. Amino Acids
  • Amino acids are building blocks of proteins.
  • Twenty standard amino acids are commonly used in protein synthesis.
  • Some amino acids are essential in the human diet.
  • Others can be synthesised by the body.
71. Peptide Bond
  • Peptide bond links amino acids.
  • It forms between the amino group of one amino acid and carboxyl group of another.
  • Many peptide bonds form a polypeptide chain.
72. Lipids
  • Lipids include fats, oils, phospholipids and steroids.
  • Lipids provide concentrated energy storage.
  • Phospholipids form cell membranes.
  • Some hormones are steroid-derived.
  • Lipids are generally poorly soluble in water.
73. Fats and Oils
  • Fats are generally solid at room temperature.
  • Oils are generally liquid at room temperature.
  • Both commonly contain triglycerides.
  • Triglycerides are made from glycerol and fatty acids.
74. Nucleic Acids

Two major nucleic acids are:

  • DNA.
  • RNA.
  • They are polymers of nucleotides.
  • They store and transmit genetic information.
75. DNA
  • DNA stands for Deoxyribonucleic Acid.
  • DNA is the primary hereditary material in most organisms.
  • DNA contains deoxyribose sugar.
  • Bases are adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine.
  • DNA usually forms a double helix.
📌 Must-Memorise

DNA Bases → A, T, G, C

76. RNA
  • RNA stands for Ribonucleic Acid.
  • RNA contains ribose sugar.
  • Bases are adenine, uracil, guanine and cytosine.
  • RNA is usually single-stranded.
  • Major RNA types include mRNA, tRNA and rRNA.
📌 Must-Memorise

RNA → Uracil instead of Thymine

77. Nucleotide

A nucleotide contains:

  • Nitrogenous base.
  • Pentose sugar.
  • Phosphate group.
  • Nucleotides are building blocks of DNA and RNA.
78. ATP
  • ATP stands for Adenosine Triphosphate.
  • ATP is the major immediate energy-transfer molecule in cells.
  • Energy released during metabolism is captured in ATP.
  • ATP contains adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ATP → Energy Currency of Cell

79. Enzyme
  • Enzymes are biological catalysts.
  • They increase reaction rate.
  • They lower activation energy.
  • They are not consumed permanently in the reaction.
  • Most enzymes are proteins.
  • Some RNA molecules can act as enzymes and are called ribozymes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Enzyme → Biological Catalyst

80. Enzyme Specificity
  • Enzymes are generally specific for particular substrates or reactions.
  • Active site binds the substrate.
  • Shape and chemical properties of the active site determine specificity.
81. Factors Affecting Enzymes

Important factors include:

  • Temperature.
  • pH.
  • Substrate concentration.
  • Enzyme concentration.
  • Inhibitors.
  • Cofactors.
82. Temperature and Enzymes
  • Enzyme activity generally increases with temperature up to an optimum.
  • Excessive heat can denature proteins.
  • Low temperature generally slows enzyme reactions without necessarily destroying the enzyme.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

High Heat → Enzyme Denaturation

83. pH and Enzymes
  • Different enzymes have different optimum pH values.
  • Pepsin works best in acidic conditions.
  • Trypsin works best in alkaline conditions of the small intestine.
  • Extreme pH can alter enzyme structure.
84. Denaturation
  • Denaturation is loss of a protein's normal three-dimensional structure.
  • Heat, extreme pH and chemicals can cause denaturation.
  • Denatured enzymes often lose catalytic activity.
  • Denaturation does not usually break all peptide bonds.
85. Diffusion
  • Diffusion is movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration due to random molecular motion.
  • It does not require cellular energy.
  • Oxygen and carbon dioxide can move across membranes by diffusion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diffusion → High to Low Concentration

86. Osmosis
  • Osmosis is net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
  • Water moves from higher water potential toward lower water potential.
  • In school-level terms, water moves from dilute solution toward concentrated solution across a semipermeable membrane.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Osmosis → Water Movement through Selectively Permeable Membrane

87. Active Transport
  • Active transport moves substances against a concentration or electrochemical gradient.
  • It requires cellular energy.
  • Membrane proteins act as pumps or transporters.
  • Sodium-potassium pump is a major animal-cell example.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Active Transport → Energy Required

88. Endocytosis
  • Endocytosis brings material into a cell using membrane-bound vesicles.
  • Phagocytosis engulfs large particles.
  • Pinocytosis takes in extracellular fluid.
  • Amoeba feeds partly by phagocytosis.
89. Exocytosis
  • Exocytosis releases substances from cells.
  • Vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane.
  • Hormones, enzymes and neurotransmitters can be secreted by exocytosis.
90. Cell Division

Two major types are:

  • Mitosis.
  • Meiosis.
  • Cell division is essential for growth, repair and reproduction.
91. Cell Cycle

Main stages include:

  • Interphase.
  • M phase.

Interphase includes:

  • G₁.
  • S.
  • G₂.
  • DNA replication occurs during S phase.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

DNA Replication → S Phase

92. Mitosis
  • Mitosis produces two genetically similar daughter cells in basic conditions.
  • Chromosome number is maintained.
  • It occurs in somatic cells.
  • It supports growth, tissue repair and asexual reproduction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mitosis → 2 Cells → Same Chromosome Number

93. Stages of Mitosis

Main stages are:

  • Prophase.
  • Metaphase.
  • Anaphase.
  • Telophase.
📌 Memory

PMAT

94. Prophase
  • Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes.
  • Mitotic spindle develops.
  • Nuclear envelope breaks down during late prophase/prometaphase in many cells.
95. Metaphase
  • Chromosomes align near the cell equator.
  • Spindle fibres attach to chromosome kinetochores.
  • Chromosomes are most condensed and easy to observe.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Metaphase → Chromosomes at Equator

96. Anaphase
  • Sister chromatids separate.
  • They move toward opposite poles.
  • Each separated chromatid becomes a daughter chromosome.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anaphase → Chromatids Separate

97. Telophase
  • Chromosomes reach opposite poles.
  • Nuclear envelopes reform.
  • Chromosomes begin to decondense.
  • Cytokinesis usually follows or overlaps.
98. Cytokinesis
  • Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
  • Animal cells usually form a cleavage furrow.
  • Plant cells form a cell plate.
  • The cell plate develops into a new separating cell wall.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Animal cytokinesis → Cleavage furrow.

Plant cytokinesis → Cell plate.

99. Meiosis
  • Meiosis produces cells with half the original chromosome number.
  • It involves two successive divisions.
  • One diploid cell generally produces four haploid cells.
  • It occurs during gamete formation in animals.
  • Meiosis creates genetic variation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Meiosis → 4 Haploid Cells

100. Meiosis I and II
  • Meiosis I is reductional division.
  • Homologous chromosomes separate.
  • Meiosis II resembles mitosis in separating sister chromatids.
  • DNA replicates before meiosis I but not between meiosis I and meiosis II.
101. Crossing Over
  • Crossing over occurs between homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
  • It exchanges DNA segments.
  • It creates new combinations of alleles.
  • Crossing over contributes to genetic variation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Crossing Over → Prophase I

102. Haploid and Diploid
  • Haploid cells contain one set of chromosomes.
  • Symbol → n.
  • Diploid cells contain two chromosome sets.
  • Symbol → 2n.
  • Human gametes are haploid.
  • Most human somatic cells are diploid.
103. Tissue
  • A tissue is a group of similar cells performing a common function.
  • Plants and animals possess specialised tissues.
  • Histology is the study of tissues.
104. Plant Tissues

Broad types are:

  • Meristematic tissue.
  • Permanent tissue.
105. Meristematic Tissue
  • Meristematic cells divide actively.
  • They are responsible for plant growth.
  • Apical meristem increases length.
  • Lateral meristem increases girth.
  • Intercalary meristem contributes to growth at internodes or leaf bases in some plants.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Apical Meristem → Length

Lateral Meristem → Girth

106. Permanent Plant Tissue

Simple permanent tissues include:

  • Parenchyma.
  • Collenchyma.
  • Sclerenchyma.

Complex permanent tissues include:

  • Xylem.
  • Phloem.
107. Parenchyma
  • Parenchyma cells are generally living.
  • They have relatively thin walls.
  • They perform storage, photosynthesis and repair.
  • Chlorenchyma is photosynthetic parenchyma.
  • Aerenchyma contains large air spaces.
108. Collenchyma
  • Collenchyma consists of living elongated cells.
  • Cell walls are unevenly thickened.
  • It provides flexible mechanical support.
  • It is common in young stems and leaf stalks.
109. Sclerenchyma
  • Sclerenchyma cells are usually dead at maturity.
  • Their walls are thick and lignified.
  • They provide strong mechanical support.
  • Fibres and sclereids are forms of sclerenchyma.
110. Xylem
  • Xylem transports water and minerals mainly from roots upward.
  • It also provides mechanical support.
  • Vessels and tracheids are important conducting cells.
  • Xylem is mostly composed of dead cells at maturity except xylem parenchyma.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Xylem → Water + Minerals

111. Phloem
  • Phloem transports organic food, especially sugars.
  • Transport can occur from source to sink in different directions depending on plant needs.
  • Sieve-tube elements and companion cells are important phloem cells.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phloem → Food/Sugar Transport

112. Animal Tissues

Four basic animal tissue types are:

  • Epithelial.
  • Connective.
  • Muscular.
  • Nervous.
📌 Must-Memorise

Animal Tissues → Epithelial + Connective + Muscle + Nervous

113. Epithelial Tissue
  • Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces.
  • It lines internal cavities and organs.
  • It forms many glands.
  • Functions include protection, absorption, secretion and exchange.
114. Connective Tissue
  • Connective tissue supports, binds and connects other tissues.
  • Examples include blood, bone, cartilage, adipose tissue and tendons.
  • It generally contains cells embedded in extracellular matrix.
115. Blood as Connective Tissue
  • Blood is a fluid connective tissue.
  • Plasma is its liquid matrix.
  • Formed elements include red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
  • Blood transports gases, nutrients, hormones and wastes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blood → Connective Tissue

116. Muscle Tissue

Three major muscle types are:

  • Skeletal.
  • Smooth.
  • Cardiac.
117. Skeletal Muscle
  • Skeletal muscle is striated.
  • It is mostly under voluntary control.
  • It attaches to bones.
  • It enables body movement.
118. Smooth Muscle
  • Smooth muscle is non-striated.
  • It is involuntary.
  • It occurs in walls of organs such as intestine and blood vessels.
119. Cardiac Muscle
  • Cardiac muscle forms the heart wall.
  • It is striated.
  • It is involuntary.
  • Cells are branched and connected by intercalated discs.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cardiac muscle → Striated but involuntary.

120. Nervous Tissue
  • Nervous tissue receives and transmits electrical signals.
  • Neurons are specialised nerve cells.
  • Glial cells support and protect neurons.
  • Brain, spinal cord and nerves contain nervous tissue.
121. Neuron

Main parts include:

  • Cell body.
  • Dendrites.
  • Axon.
  • Dendrites mainly receive signals.
  • Axon carries impulses away from the cell body.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dendrite → Receives

Axon → Carries Away

122. Organ
  • An organ contains two or more tissue types working together.
  • Heart is an organ.
  • Leaf is a plant organ.
  • Kidney is an organ.
  • Stomach is an organ.
123. Organ System
  • An organ system is a group of organs working together.
  • Digestive system.
  • Respiratory system.
  • Circulatory system.
  • Nervous system.
  • Excretory system.
  • Reproductive system.
124. Photosynthesis
  • Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy.
  • Green plants use carbon dioxide and water.
  • Oxygen is released as a by-product.
  • Chlorophyll absorbs light.
  • Photosynthesis occurs mainly in chloroplasts.
📌 Simplified Equation

6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

in the presence of light and chlorophyll.

125. Chlorophyll
  • Chlorophyll is the major green photosynthetic pigment.
  • It absorbs mainly red and blue wavelengths.
  • It reflects more green light.
  • Magnesium is present at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chlorophyll → Magnesium

126. Stomata
  • Stomata are microscopic pores mainly in leaf epidermis.
  • Guard cells regulate their opening.
  • Stomata allow gas exchange.
  • Water vapour exits through stomata during transpiration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stomata → Gas Exchange + Transpiration

127. Transpiration
  • Transpiration is loss of water vapour from aerial parts of plants.
  • Most transpiration occurs through stomata.
  • It helps create a pull for water movement through xylem.
  • It also contributes to leaf cooling.
128. Tropism
  • Tropism is directional growth response of a plant to a stimulus.
  • Phototropism → Response to light.
  • Geotropism/gravitropism → Response to gravity.
  • Hydrotropism → Response to water.
  • Thigmotropism → Response to touch.
129. Phototropism
  • Shoots generally show positive phototropism.
  • They grow toward light.
  • Auxin redistribution contributes to bending.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shoot → Positive Phototropism

130. Gravitropism
  • Roots generally show positive gravitropism.
  • Shoots generally show negative gravitropism.
  • Gravity influences auxin distribution and growth.
131. Plant Hormones

Major plant hormones include:

  • Auxins.
  • Gibberellins.
  • Cytokinins.
  • Abscisic acid.
  • Ethylene.
132. Auxin
  • Auxin promotes cell elongation in shoots.
  • It plays a role in phototropism.
  • It promotes apical dominance.
  • Indole-3-acetic acid is an important natural auxin.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Auxin → Cell Elongation + Apical Dominance

133. Gibberellin
  • Gibberellins promote stem elongation.
  • They promote seed germination in many plants.
  • They can promote flowering and fruit growth in selected species.
134. Cytokinin
  • Cytokinins promote cell division.
  • They can delay leaf senescence.
  • They interact with auxins in plant growth and development.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cytokinin → Cell Division

135. Abscisic Acid
  • Abscisic acid is abbreviated ABA.
  • It promotes stomatal closure during water stress.
  • It contributes to seed dormancy.
  • It generally acts as a growth-inhibiting/stress hormone in basic classification.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ABA → Stomatal Closure + Dormancy

136. Ethylene
  • Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone.
  • It promotes fruit ripening.
  • It participates in leaf and fruit abscission.
  • It also influences stress responses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ethylene → Fruit Ripening

137. Biological Organisation Levels

A common sequence is:

Atom → Molecule → Organelle → Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ System → Organism → Population → Community → Ecosystem → Biosphere

138. Species
  • A species is a basic unit of biological classification.
  • In the biological species concept, members can interbreed naturally and produce fertile offspring.
  • This definition has limitations for asexual organisms and fossils.
139. Population
  • A population consists of individuals of the same species living in a particular area.
  • Population size changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration.
140. Community
  • A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
141. Ecosystem
  • An ecosystem includes a biological community and its physical environment.
  • Energy flows through ecosystems.
  • Nutrients are recycled.
  • Producers, consumers and decomposers are major functional groups.
142. Producers
  • Producers synthesise organic food from inorganic substances.
  • Green plants are major producers.
  • Algae and cyanobacteria are also important producers.
143. Consumers
  • Consumers obtain energy by eating other organisms.
  • Herbivores are primary consumers.
  • Carnivores may occupy secondary or higher trophic levels.
  • Omnivores eat both plant and animal material.
144. Decomposers
  • Decomposers break down dead organic matter.
  • Bacteria and fungi are major decomposers.
  • They recycle nutrients back into ecosystems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Decomposers → Bacteria + Fungi

145. Gene
  • A gene is a functional unit of heredity.
  • Genes consist of DNA in cellular organisms.
  • Genes influence traits through RNA and protein production.
  • Genes are located on chromosomes.
146. Heredity
  • Heredity is transmission of biological traits from parents to offspring.
  • DNA carries hereditary information.
  • Genetics is the study of heredity and variation.
  • Gregor Mendel is called the Father of Genetics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gregor Mendel → Father of Genetics

147. Variation
  • Variation means differences among individuals.
  • Variation may be genetic or environmental.
  • Genetic variation provides raw material for evolution.
  • Mutation and recombination generate genetic variation.
148. Evolution
  • Biological evolution is change in inherited characteristics of populations across generations.
  • Natural selection is an important mechanism of evolution.
  • Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the principle of natural selection.
  • Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Darwin → Natural Selection → 1859

149. Mutation
  • Mutation is a change in genetic material.
  • Mutations can occur spontaneously or be induced.
  • They may be harmful, neutral or beneficial.
  • Mutations are a source of genetic variation.
150. Virus — Life Science Link
  • Viruses are acellular infectious agents.
  • They contain genetic material surrounded by a protein coat.
  • Some also have lipid envelopes.
  • Viruses cannot reproduce independently.
  • They replicate only inside living host cells.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Virus → Acellular and obligate intracellular parasite.

151. Virus Genetic Material
  • A virus contains either DNA or RNA as its genome.
  • A single virus particle does not normally contain both DNA and RNA as its genetic genome.
  • Retroviruses such as HIV contain RNA genomes.
152. Bacteria
  • Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotes.
  • They reproduce mainly by binary fission.
  • Some are useful.
  • Some cause disease.
  • Bacteria have 70S ribosomes.
  • Most possess peptidoglycan cell walls.
153. Binary Fission
  • Binary fission is an asexual reproductive process.
  • One cell divides into two daughter cells.
  • Bacteria commonly reproduce by binary fission.
  • Amoeba also reproduces by binary fission.
154. Fungi
  • Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs.
  • Their cell walls contain chitin.
  • They absorb nutrients from surroundings.
  • Yeast is unicellular.
  • Mushrooms and moulds are multicellular fungi.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fungal Cell Wall → Chitin

155. Protists
  • Protists are mostly unicellular or simple eukaryotes in traditional classification.
  • Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena are common textbook examples.
  • Modern classification recognises multiple evolutionary lineages within organisms traditionally grouped as Protista.
156. Scientific Naming
  • Binomial nomenclature gives each species a two-part scientific name.
  • First part → Genus.
  • Second part → Specific epithet.
  • Genus begins with a capital letter.
  • Specific epithet begins with a lowercase letter.
  • Scientific names are italicised when printed.
📌 Example

Homo sapiens

157. Carl Linnaeus
  • Carl Linnaeus formalised binomial nomenclature.
  • He is called the Father of Taxonomy.
  • His Systema Naturae was highly influential.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Linnaeus → Father of Taxonomy

158. Taxonomy
  • Taxonomy deals with identification, nomenclature and classification of organisms.
  • Classical hierarchy includes:
  • Kingdom.
  • Phylum/Division.
  • Class.
  • Order.
  • Family.
  • Genus.
  • Species.
📌 Memory

Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species

159. Microscopy
  • Microscopes magnify objects too small for the naked eye.
  • Light microscopes use visible light.
  • Electron microscopes use electron beams.
  • Electron microscopes have much greater resolving power than light microscopes.
160. TEM
  • TEM stands for Transmission Electron Microscope.
  • Electrons pass through very thin specimens.
  • It reveals internal ultrastructure.
  • TEM gives extremely high-resolution images.
161. SEM
  • SEM stands for Scanning Electron Microscope.
  • It scans specimen surfaces with electrons.
  • It provides detailed surface images with three-dimensional appearance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

TEM → Internal Structure

SEM → Surface

162. Resolution
  • Resolution is the ability to distinguish two nearby points as separate.
  • A microscope with high resolution reveals finer detail.
  • Magnification without resolution does not produce useful new detail.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Magnification ≠ Resolution.

163. Life Science — Important Scientist Pairs
  • Aristotle → Zoology.
  • Theophrastus → Botany.
  • Robert Hooke → Cell.
  • Leeuwenhoek → Living microorganisms.
  • Schleiden → Plant cell theory.
  • Schwann → Animal cell theory.
  • Virchow → Cells from pre-existing cells.
  • Linnaeus → Taxonomy.
  • Mendel → Genetics.
  • Darwin → Evolution by natural selection.
  • Singer and Nicolson → Fluid mosaic model.
  • Christian de Duve → Lysosome.
  • Camillo Golgi → Golgi apparatus.
  • Lynn Margulis → Endosymbiotic theory.
164. Important Dates
  • Hooke observed cork cells → 1665.
  • Schleiden plant-cell idea → 1838.
  • Schwann animal-cell theory → 1839.
  • Darwin's Origin of Species → 1859.
  • Mendel's pea experiments published → 1866.
  • Fluid mosaic model → 1972.
165. Must-Memorise Cell Organelle Functions
  • Nucleus → Genetic control.
  • Nucleolus → Ribosome formation.
  • Mitochondria → ATP production.
  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis.
  • Rough ER → Protein synthesis/processing.
  • Smooth ER → Lipid synthesis/detoxification.
  • Golgi → Modification/packaging.
  • Lysosome → Digestion.
  • Chloroplast → Photosynthesis.
  • Vacuole → Storage/turgor.
  • Peroxisome → H₂O₂ breakdown.
166. Must-Memorise Biomolecule Pairs
  • Carbohydrate → Major energy source.
  • Protein → Amino acids.
  • Lipid → Long-term energy/membranes.
  • DNA → Genetic information.
  • RNA → Protein-expression roles.
  • ATP → Immediate energy currency.
  • Enzyme → Biological catalyst.
167. Must-Memorise Tissue Pairs
  • Xylem → Water/minerals.
  • Phloem → Food.
  • Parenchyma → Storage.
  • Collenchyma → Flexible support.
  • Sclerenchyma → Strong support.
  • Epithelial → Covering/lining.
  • Connective → Support/binding.
  • Muscle → Movement.
  • Nervous → Impulse transmission.
168. TNPSC Traps
  • Cell is the basic unit of life.
  • Hooke observed cork cells in 1665.
  • Leeuwenhoek observed living microorganisms.
  • Schleiden → Plants.
  • Schwann → Animals.
  • Virchow → Pre-existing cells.
  • Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
  • Bacteria are prokaryotes.
  • Fungi are eukaryotes.
  • Plant cell wall → Cellulose.
  • Fungal cell wall → Chitin.
  • Bacterial wall → Peptidoglycan.
  • Ribosome is not membrane-bound.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain 70S-like ribosomes.
  • Cytoplasmic eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S.
  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis.
  • Golgi → Packaging.
  • Lysosome → Intracellular digestion.
  • Smooth ER → Lipids.
  • Rough ER → Proteins.
  • Human somatic cells → 46 chromosomes.
  • Human gametes → 23.
  • DNA uses thymine.
  • RNA uses uracil.
  • Plant storage carbohydrate → Starch.
  • Animal storage carbohydrate → Glycogen.
  • Plant cell wall carbohydrate → Cellulose.
  • Magnesium is central to chlorophyll.
  • ATP is the cellular energy currency.
  • Diffusion does not require metabolic energy.
  • Active transport requires energy.
  • Mitosis maintains chromosome number.
  • Meiosis halves chromosome number.
  • Crossing over occurs in prophase I.
  • Plant cytokinesis → Cell plate.
  • Animal cytokinesis → Cleavage furrow.
  • Xylem → Water.
  • Phloem → Food.
  • Blood is connective tissue.
  • Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary.
  • Dendrite receives; axon carries impulses away.
  • Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts.
  • Respiration is not the same as breathing.
  • Excretion is not the same as egestion.
  • Viruses are acellular.
  • Bt bacterium is living; viruses require host cells for replication.
  • Linnaeus → Taxonomy.
  • Mendel → Genetics.
  • Darwin → Natural selection.
169. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Biology → Life.
  • Cell → Basic unit.
  • Hooke → 1665.
  • Leeuwenhoek → Microorganisms.
  • Schleiden → Plant cells.
  • Schwann → Animal cells.
  • Virchow → Existing cells.
  • Prokaryote → No true nucleus.
  • Eukaryote → True nucleus.
  • Plant wall → Cellulose.
  • Fungus wall → Chitin.
  • Bacterium wall → Peptidoglycan.
  • Mitochondria → ATP.
  • Ribosome → Protein.
  • Golgi → Package.
  • Lysosome → Digest.
  • Chloroplast → Photosynthesis.
  • DNA → A T G C.
  • RNA → A U G C.
  • ATP → Energy.
  • Mitosis → 2 same.
  • Meiosis → 4 haploid.
  • Crossing over → Prophase I.
  • Xylem → Water.
  • Phloem → Food.
  • Blood → Connective.
  • Mg → Chlorophyll.
  • Auxin → Elongation.
  • Cytokinin → Division.
  • ABA → Dormancy.
  • Ethylene → Ripening.
  • Mendel → Genetics.
  • Darwin → Evolution.
  • Linnaeus → Taxonomy.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Biology means? → Study of life.
  • Father of Botany? → Theophrastus.
  • Father of Zoology? → Aristotle.
  • Basic structural and functional unit of life? → Cell.
  • Who coined the term cell after observing cork? → Robert Hooke.
  • Year Hooke observed cork cells? → 1665.
  • Who first observed living microorganisms? → Antonie van Leeuwenhoek.
  • Father of Microbiology commonly called? → Leeuwenhoek.
  • Who proposed plants are made of cells? → Matthias Schleiden.
  • Who extended cell theory to animals? → Theodor Schwann.
  • Who stated cells arise from pre-existing cells? → Rudolf Virchow.
  • Latin phrase associated with Virchow? → Omnis cellula e cellula.
  • What is a prokaryote? → Organism whose cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
  • Examples of prokaryotes? → Bacteria and archaea.
  • Eukaryotes possess? → Membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.
  • Prokaryotic ribosome? → 70S.
  • Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosome? → 80S.
  • Plant cell-wall material? → Cellulose.
  • Fungal cell-wall material? → Chitin.
  • Bacterial cell-wall material commonly? → Peptidoglycan.
  • Plasma membrane property? → Selectively permeable.
  • Fluid mosaic model proposed by? → Singer and Nicolson.
  • Year? → 1972.
  • Organelle containing most eukaryotic DNA? → Nucleus.
  • Nucleolus function? → Ribosome formation.
  • Powerhouse of cell? → Mitochondrion.
  • Site of protein synthesis? → Ribosome.
  • Rough ER mainly associated with? → Protein synthesis.
  • Smooth ER mainly associated with? → Lipid synthesis and detoxification.
  • Golgi apparatus function? → Modification, sorting and packaging.
  • Lysosome function? → Intracellular digestion.
  • Who discovered lysosomes? → Christian de Duve.
  • Chloroplast function? → Photosynthesis.
  • Plant central vacuole function? → Storage and turgor.
  • Organelle breaking down hydrogen peroxide? → Peroxisome.
  • Human somatic chromosome number? → 46.
  • Number of chromosome pairs in humans? → 23.
  • Human gamete chromosome number? → 23.
  • Main plant-storage carbohydrate? → Starch.
  • Main animal-storage carbohydrate? → Glycogen.
  • Plant structural polysaccharide? → Cellulose.
  • Protein made from? → Amino acids.
  • Bond joining amino acids? → Peptide bond.
  • Triglyceride made from? → Glycerol + fatty acids.
  • DNA full form? → Deoxyribonucleic Acid.
  • DNA bases? → Adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine.
  • RNA full form? → Ribonucleic Acid.
  • RNA base replacing thymine? → Uracil.
  • Basic unit of DNA/RNA? → Nucleotide.
  • ATP full form? → Adenosine Triphosphate.
  • ATP function? → Immediate cellular energy transfer.
  • Enzyme means? → Biological catalyst.
  • Do enzymes increase activation energy? → No, they lower it.
  • High temperature can cause enzyme? → Denaturation.
  • Diffusion direction? → High concentration to low concentration.
  • Osmosis specifically involves movement of? → Water.
  • Does active transport require energy? → Yes.
  • DNA replication occurs during which cell-cycle phase? → S phase.
  • Mitosis produces? → Two genetically similar daughter cells.
  • Main mitotic stages? → Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
  • PMAT stands for? → Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase.
  • Chromosomes line up at equator during? → Metaphase.
  • Sister chromatids separate during? → Anaphase.
  • Plant cytokinesis forms? → Cell plate.
  • Animal cytokinesis forms? → Cleavage furrow.
  • Meiosis produces? → Four haploid cells in the basic model.
  • Reductional division? → Meiosis I.
  • Crossing over occurs during? → Prophase I of meiosis.
  • Haploid symbol? → n.
  • Diploid symbol? → 2n.
  • Plant meristem increasing length? → Apical meristem.
  • Meristem increasing girth? → Lateral meristem.
  • Simple permanent tissues? → Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
  • Xylem transports? → Water and minerals.
  • Phloem transports? → Organic food/sugars.
  • Four basic animal tissues? → Epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.
  • Blood belongs to which tissue? → Connective tissue.
  • Three muscle types? → Skeletal, smooth and cardiac.
  • Which muscle is striated and voluntary? → Skeletal.
  • Which is non-striated and involuntary? → Smooth.
  • Which is striated and involuntary? → Cardiac.
  • Basic nerve cell? → Neuron.
  • Dendrite function? → Receives signals.
  • Axon function? → Carries impulses away from cell body.
  • Photosynthesis occurs mainly in? → Chloroplast.
  • Photosynthetic pigment? → Chlorophyll.
  • Central atom in chlorophyll? → Magnesium.
  • Raw materials of photosynthesis? → Carbon dioxide and water.
  • Gas released during photosynthesis? → Oxygen.
  • Stomata function? → Gas exchange and transpiration.
  • Main water-conducting tissue? → Xylem.
  • Plant hormone for cell elongation? → Auxin.
  • Plant hormone promoting cell division? → Cytokinin.
  • Hormone associated with stem elongation? → Gibberellin.
  • Hormone associated with dormancy and stomatal closure? → Abscisic acid.
  • Gaseous plant hormone for fruit ripening? → Ethylene.
  • Autotroph means? → Organism producing its own organic food from inorganic sources.
  • Saprotroph means? → Feeds on dead organic matter by external digestion.
  • Example of parasitic plant? → Cuscuta.
  • Respiration vs breathing? → Respiration is biochemical energy release; breathing is gas movement.
  • Main site of aerobic ATP production? → Mitochondria.
  • Excretion means? → Removal of metabolic wastes.
  • Egestion means? → Removal of undigested food.
  • Organisms that recycle dead matter? → Decomposers.
  • Main decomposers? → Bacteria and fungi.
  • Unit of heredity? → Gene.
  • Father of Genetics? → Gregor Mendel.
  • Natural-selection scientist? → Charles Darwin.
  • Darwin's Origin of Species year? → 1859.
  • Father of Taxonomy? → Carl Linnaeus.
  • Scientific naming system? → Binomial nomenclature.
  • First part of scientific name? → Genus.
  • Second part? → Specific epithet.
  • Virus is cellular or acellular? → Acellular.
  • Can viruses reproduce independently? → No.
  • Bacteria are prokaryotic or eukaryotic? → Prokaryotic.
  • Fungi are prokaryotic or eukaryotic? → Eukaryotic.
  • TEM mainly shows? → Internal ultrastructure.
  • SEM mainly shows? → Surface details.
  • Resolution means? → Ability to distinguish two close points separately.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Hooke → cell; Leeuwenhoek → microorganisms; Mitochondria → ATP; Ribosome → protein; Chloroplast → photosynthesis; Xylem → water; Phloem → food; Mitosis → 2 diploid-like cells; Meiosis → 4 haploid cells.
